title: Treating PTSD is a Good Idea
subtitle: Please, take it seriously!
body_html:
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) has one of the best brands of all psychiatric disorders. It doesn't mean you're crazy, it means something bad happened to you. The person largely responsible for this is a man named Bessel Van Der Kolk, who I'm happy to call a friend.

He wrote a book called “The Body Keeps the Score” (amazon affiliate link) which is so outrageously popular that most versions of the book are excluded from the Amazon affiliate marketing program.

It goes to show, if you want to change the world, write a book about something. It's no guarantee that it'll work, and maybe you should make a TikTok video instead, I don't know. But this book helped put post-traumatic stress disorder on the map as something that wasn't just a problem for your brain, but it was a problem for your whole body.

I'm gonna start by explaining a little bit about what trauma does to our brains and bodies, and why it does that.

When something happens that could harm you, could kill you, could kill somebody else right in front of you, could violate your right to live free of coercion, violence, sexual assault, and the like? We have a biological system to help keep us alive. When something tried to kill us once, it makes sense to not forget it. You should remember it better than anything else you have ever remembered, from an evolutionary standpoint? If you survived a life-threatening event once? Well, you might have to again.

We learned to mobilize our fight or flight responses so that we didn't die then, and so that we won't die next time. This system has to work flawlessly, or we don't have kids, and nobody can learn the lesson in the future. If you don't escape a life-threatening anything, you're dead.

Our sympathetic nervous system mobilizes our entire body to respond to potential trauma, and avoid that experience in the future. Some experiences, however, we can't control, and we can't escape. These which pair, powerlessness and threat are particularly bad. In these circumstances, we need to escape, via dissociation, into our own minds, because to sit there and be completely in the moment while someone is assaulting you is both physically and psychologically intolerable. Posttraumatic stress disorder exist because our trauma response saved our life once. This response, built into our biology, evolved in the context of tigers maybe eating us—infrequently.

We didn't evolve to cope with chronic stress and chronic trauma, and yet for any of us, that's what we're exposed to, in childhood, particularly.

Share

It's not adaptive to respond to everyday situations, as if they were trauma, however, responding to everything like it might kill you keeps you on the edge of your seat, and maybe you're not functional, but at least you didn't get eaten by a tiger.

There is a relentless logic to our experience of trauma, we need to escape, we need to dissociate, and even when it's just something that's close enough, like the sound of a car, horn honking, or someone who looks a lot like the guy who attacked us? Any of these things can trigger our traumas.

Social exclusion can be just as traumatizing as physical threat1. And now, we carry social exclusion, or the possibility of it around with us all the time in our pocket. Thanks, the Internet. This can have real consequences, even in experimental paradigms:

Besides higher levels of perceived social exclusion, participants in the exclusion condition reported higher ill-being than those in the inclusion condition (with no significant differences observed in terms of the other outcomes). Results further showed childhood trauma to be positively associated with emotion dysregulation and ill-being, and negatively associated with need satisfaction and well-being2.

It's a source of constant threat, constant stress, and constant ability to remind us that somewhere, somehow, to someone who reminds us of ourselves, something traumatic is happening. Thank goodness, there are more treatments now than ever.

There is hope for PTSD, available both now and more coming soon.

I’ve written prior articles about the impact of trauma. My friend wrote some punch articles on the topic too:

And I’ve written about it’s treatment options:

Some treatments don’t work: Does Medical Cannabis work for PTSD? Spoiler alert: not really. MDMA’s failure in it’s first round of trials to play by the rules of the FDA and ethical trial conduct has been extensively reported here.

The late Nolan Williams, M.D., did breathaking work on Ibogaine and it’s potential (combined with magnesium for safety) for PTSD in co-occuring TBI. Compass has submitted to the FDA for a COMP360 indication in PTSD as well.

Available Now?

Also available now: PRISM EEG-fMRI biomarker neurofeedback. It works really well, and has no significant risk.

Since nightmares are common—and increase the risk of suicide— it’s nice to know we have access to FDA-breakthroughs like Nightware. Prazosin does work for PTSD-related nightmares.

Shan Siddiqi, M.D., is studying PTSD specific fMRI-guided accelerated TMS as we speak, to make this available at scale, along with colleagues from Acacia Clinics.

If you are suffering, or know someone who is, we have these options available at Radial, where I work.

Learn About Care at Radial

1

Olson MD. The Influence of Social Exclusion on Posttraumatic Stress Reactions in Older Adult Veterans. Soc Work. 2020 Apr 1;65(2):123-130. doi: 10.1093/sw/swaa008. PMID: 32211796.

2

Rashid, A., Costa, S. & van der Kaap-Deeder, J. The effects of social exclusion on emotion regulation, basic needs, well-being, and ill-being: examining the moderating role of childhood trauma. Humanit Soc Sci Commun 12, 1993 (2025). https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-025-06220-w
